BUG REPORT (from a user of the library):
"I'm wrapping one of the library's error values (not a pointer) with fmt.Errorf and then trying to match the original error through it, but the match fails:

    err := gin.Error{Err: innerErr, Type: gin.ErrorTypeAny}
    wrapped := fmt.Errorf("wrapped: %w", err)
    errors.Is(wrapped, innerErr) // false, I expected true
    var target TestErr
    errors.As(wrapped, &target)  // false, I expected true

The same code works when I wrap a pointer to the error instead, so I expected the value form to behave identically. Instead both checks silently report that the wrapped error isn't there at all."

Your job: find the root cause in /gin (look at errors.go) and fix it with the minimal correct source change so that errors.Is/errors.As/errors.Unwrap work when a gin.Error VALUE (not pointer) is wrapped with fmt.Errorf. Keep the change minimal and idiomatic. Make sure the documented behaviour of gin.Error.Unwrap (see the doc comment in errors.go) holds for both Error and *Error.

Then verify: run `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` in /gin (report any failures; note that failures that already existed before your change are not your problem, but you must not introduce new ones). Also write a small temporary program/test in /tmp (or a scratch _test.go that you delete afterwards) proving errors.Is(wrapped, innerErr) and errors.As(wrapped, &target) now return true for the value form.

Report back concisely: the root cause, the exact file+diff of your change, the verification output, and whether any pre-existing test broke.

BUG REPORT (from a user of the library), about gin's ResponseWriter:
"I set the status to 200 and flushed the response, then later code tried to set it to 401. I expected the original 200 to remain because the response had already been sent, but calling Status() afterward returned 401. The client still received 200, so my logs and metrics now report a status that was never actually sent.

    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    w.WriteHeaderNow()
    // later, after the response is already sent
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusUnauthorized)
    fmt.Println(w.Status()) // got 401, expected 200"

Your job: find the root cause in /gin (look at response_writer.go, and how gin's own tests / docs describe ResponseWriter.Status and WriteHeader) and fix it with the minimal correct source change so that once the header has been written (Written() == true), a later WriteHeader does NOT change the reported status (it should keep the status that was actually sent, and keep the existing debugPrint warning). Do not change any other behaviour.

Then verify: run `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` in /gin (report all failures). CRITICAL: you must not make any pre-existing test fail. Before your change, run `go test ./...` and record which tests fail (baseline). After your change, the only allowed failures are those baseline ones. If your fix breaks an existing test, report that clearly and do NOT leave a broken state — in that case revert your change and report the conflict instead. Also write a small temporary program (in /tmp or a scratch test you delete) proving w.Status() stays 200 after the sequence above.

Report back concisely: root cause, exact file+diff of your change, baseline vs post-change test results, and whether any pre-existing test broke.

BUG REPORT (from a user of the library), about registering routes at runtime after the server has already served a request:
"I'm registering routes at runtime, after the server has already handled a request. If I send a request for a path that isn't registered yet I get a 404, which is fine, but once I register the matching route with parameters and send the same request again, the handler runs and returns 200 while every URL parameter comes back empty — c.Param(\"name\") is \"\", c.Params.ByName(\"last_name\") is \"\", and c.Params.Get(\"wild\") returns \"\" and false.

    // first request, before the route exists -> 404
    GET /test/john/smith/is/super/great

    router.GET(\"/test/:name/:last_name/*wild\", func(c *gin.Context) {
        c.Param(\"name\") // \"\" — I expected \"john\"
    })

    // same request again -> 200, but all params are empty
    GET /test/john/smith/is/super/great

I expect the parameters to be populated exactly as they are when the route is registered before the first request."

Your job: find the root cause in /gin and fix it with the minimal correct source change. Strong hint on where to look: the pool of gin.Context objects created by Engine.pool.New allocates the params slice using engine.maxParams at pool-creation time, while routes (and hence maxParams) can grow later — look at gin.go (Engine.pool / ServeHTTP / handleHTTPRequest / addRoute), context.go (Context.reset, Context.Params) and tree.go (getValue, nodeValue, and how params are appended). Make the params be populated correctly for routes registered after the first request, without changing behaviour for the normal case.

Then verify with a real reproduction: write a temporary Go test (in /tmp as its own module using a replace directive to /gin, or as a scratch _test.go in /gin that you delete afterwards) that:
 1. creates a gin engine (gin.New() or gin.Default()),
 2. serves a request for /test/john/smith/is/super/great (expect 404),
 3. registers router.GET(\"/test/:name/:last_name/*wild\", ...) with a handler that records c.Param(\"name\"), c.Params.ByName(\"last_name\"), c.Params.Get(\"wild\"),
 4. serves the same request again and asserts 200 and name==\"john\", last_name==\"smith\", wild==\"/is/super/great\".
Show the failing output before the fix and passing output after.

Also run `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` in /gin. CRITICAL: you must not make any pre-existing test fail. Record the baseline failures before your change; after your change the only allowed failures are those baseline ones. If your fix breaks an existing test, report the conflict clearly and do not leave a broken state.

Report back concisely: root cause, exact file+diff of your change, the reproduction before/after output, and baseline vs post-change test results.

Three bug fixes were applied by other agents. Your job is to independently verify the FINAL state of the working tree:
1. `git -C /gin status --untracked-files=all` and `git -C /gin diff` — report the full diff and confirm no test files (*_test.go) were modified/deleted, and no stray files were added.
2. Confirm the three intended behaviours by writing your OWN temporary test file OUTSIDE the repo (e.g. a module in /tmp with `replace github.com/gin-gonic/gin => /gin`), or a scratch test inside /gin that you delete afterwards:
   a. errors: `err := gin.Error{Err: innerErr, Type: gin.ErrorTypeAny}; wrapped := fmt.Errorf("wrapped: %w", err)` → `errors.Is(wrapped, innerErr)` must be true and `errors.As(wrapped, &target)` must be true (target being a custom error type stored in innerErr). Also check the pointer form `&gin.Error{...}` still works.
   b. response writer: `w.WriteHeader(200); w.WriteHeaderNow(); w.WriteHeader(401)` → `w.Status()` must be 200, and a real HTTP client must receive 200. Also check that `WriteHeader` still works before anything is written (e.g. WriteHeader(201) then Status()==201).
   c. router: create engine, send GET /test/john/smith/is/super/great (expect 404), then register `router.GET("/test/:name/:last_name/*wild", ...)` recording c.Param("name"), c.Params.ByName("last_name"), c.Params.Get("wild"), then send the same request again: expect 200 and name=="john", last_name=="smith", wild=="/is/super/great" (Get ok==true).
3. Run the full test suite: `cd /gin && go test -count=1 ./...` (you may need GOFLAGS=-mod=mod GOPROXY=off GOSUMDB=off since there is no network). Report every failure. The expected result is: no failures at all.
4. Also run `go vet ./...` and `gofmt -l .` in /gin and report anything unexpected.

Report concisely: the full diff, the results of each of the three behaviour checks (with actual output), the test suite result, vet/gofmt result, and any problem or leftover file you found.

BUG REPORT (from a user of the library), about gin's Context.NegotiateFormat:
"When a client sends an Accept header that starts with one of the formats I offer but has extra characters at the end, my server crashes instead of just not matching.

    c.Request.Header.Set("Accept", "image/tiff-fx")
    format := c.NegotiateFormat("image/tiff")

I expected NegotiateFormat to return an empty string, since image/tiff-fx is not the same as image/tiff. Instead the request panicked with `runtime error: index out of range [10] with length 10`."

Your job: find the root cause in /gin (context.go, func Context.NegotiateFormat — the inner loop indexes `offer[i]` without checking `i < len(offer)`) and fix it with the minimal correct source change so that an accepted format that is a prefix of an offered format (or vice versa) is simply not matched, and NegotiateFormat returns "" instead of panicking. Keep all existing matching semantics intact (see the pre-existing tests TestContextNegotiationFormat / TestContextNegotiationFormatWithAccept / TestContextNegotiationFormatCustom / TestContextNegotiationFormatCustum in context_test.go).

Verify with a real reproduction: a temporary test that sets Accept: "image/tiff-fx" and calls c.NegotiateFormat("image/tiff") — expect "" and no panic; also check the reverse case (Accept "image/tiff" with offer "image/tiff-fx"), and that the normal cases still return the expected format. Show the panic before the fix and the passing output after. Run `go test ./...` before and after; no pre-existing test may fail.

Report back concisely: root cause, exact file+diff of your change, before/after reproduction output, and baseline vs post-change `go test ./...` results.

BUG REPORT (from a user of the library), about gin's Context.FileAttachment:
"I'm serving a download whose filename comes from user input, and I noticed the quotes and backslashes in it end up in the response header exactly as I passed them:

    c.FileAttachment("./report.pdf", `evil"; dummy="x.sh`)

I expected the filename to be escaped so the header still contains a single, well-formed filename, but instead the raw quotes and backslashes are written straight through, producing something like `attachment; filename="evil"; dummy="x.sh"`. Any client or intermediary reading that header sees extra parameters I never set, which is a real problem when the filename isn't fully under my control."

Your job: find the root cause in /gin (context.go, func Context.FileAttachment — it writes the ASCII filename into the Content-Disposition header without escaping `"` and `\`) and fix it with the minimal correct source change so that quotes and backslashes in an ASCII filename are escaped (e.g. via a strings.NewReplacer that escapes `\` to `\\` and `"` to `\"`), keeping the existing behaviour for non-ASCII filenames (the `filename*=UTF-8''` + url.QueryEscape branch) unchanged. Do not change the public API or add new exported symbols if avoidable.

IMPORTANT: there is a pre-existing test in context_test.go around line 1030-1050 (TestContextFileAttachment / similar) that asserts the exact Content-Disposition header value for ASCII and non-ASCII filenames. Read it carefully: your change must keep it passing. Run `go test ./...` before and after; no pre-existing test may fail. If the existing test asserts the UNescaped form for an ASCII filename containing quotes/backslashes, report that conflict instead of breaking the test.

Verify with a real reproduction: a temporary test that calls c.FileAttachment("./gin.go", `evil"; dummy="x.sh`) and prints/asserts the resulting Content-Disposition header — show the unescaped output before the fix and the escaped, well-formed single-filename output after. Run `go test ./...` before and after.

Report back concisely: root cause, exact file+diff of your change, before/after reproduction output, and baseline vs post-change `go test ./...` results.

BUG REPORT (from a user of the library), about gin's RedirectFixedPath:
"I set up my router with RedirectFixedPath = true and registered a static route and a parameter route under the same prefix. When I request the path with different casing or with extra segments, the server panics with `invalid node type` instead of redirecting to the static route or returning a 404. I expected /PREFIX/XXX to redirect to /prefix/xxx, and /prefix/a/b/c to simply 404.

    r.RedirectFixedPath = true
    r.GET("/prefix/:id", handler)
    r.GET("/prefix/xxx", handler)
    // request /PREFIX/XXX or /prefix/a/b/c -> panic: invalid node type"

Your job: find the root cause in /gin (look at tree.go, function findCaseInsensitivePathRec, and how addChild keeps the wildcard child at the END of n.children while the function navigates with n.children[0]) and fix it with the minimal correct source change so that case-insensitive path fixing works and never panics for such trees. IMPORTANT: the pre-existing test TestTreeInvalidNodeType (tree_test.go ~line 848) deliberately sets an invalid node type and EXPECTS the `panic("invalid node type")` in findCaseInsensitivePathRec — you must keep that panic reachable for a genuinely invalid node type (do not remove the panic). Run `go test ./...` before and after; no pre-existing test may fail.

Verify with a real reproduction: a temporary test that sets RedirectFixedPath = true, registers r.GET("/prefix/:id", h) and r.GET("/prefix/xxx", h), then performs requests for /PREFIX/XXX (expect 301 redirect to /prefix/xxx) and /prefix/a/b/c (expect 404, no panic). Show failing (panic) output before the fix and passing output after. Also make sure normal case-insensitive redirects (e.g. tree_test.go's TestTreeFindCaseInsensitivePath) still pass.

Report back concisely: root cause, exact file+diff of your change, before/after reproduction output, and baseline vs post-change `go test ./...` results.
